In a murine MHC-haploidentical HCT model, we demonstrate that prevention of GVHD with a combination of short-term VEN and CD28 costimulation blockade using ABA (VEN+ABA) was comparable to that with Cy+ABA and superior to that with Cy monotherapy, while maintaining GVL effects. Flow cytometry analysis revealed a higher regulatory T (Treg)/conventional T (Tcon) ratio with the VEN+ABA combination compared to Cy+ABA. Using donor CD8+ alloreactive TCR-transgenic T cells, we show that the VEN+ABA combination produced a prominent cleaved caspase-3 signature only in allo-activated T cells, and cells from the spleen at day 9 after HCT with VEN+ABA did not respond after ex vivo CD3/CD28 stimulation. Collectively, our study supports a VEN+ABA GVHD prophylaxis strategy associated with preferential apoptosis of alloreactive T cells while preserving GVL activity to replace alkylator-based prophylaxis.

title: Cross-Species Single-Cell, Single-Nucleus, and Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Remodeling Features of the Immune Microenvironment and Tissue Architecture Associated With Prostate Aging and Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia.
abstract: NA: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is closely associated with advancing age, but the tissue, cellular, and molecular features associated with prostate aging and BPH remain incompletely understood. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from Homo sapiens (Hsa) and Mus musculus (Mmu), single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data from Macaca fascicularis (Mfa), and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data from Hsa to characterize prostate remodeling across the available age groups. Cross-species integration using one-to-one ortholog mapping and scGen-based batch correction generated a prostate atlas comprising 47 samples and more than 400,000 cells. In species-specific analyses, CD4_Tem, CD4_Treg, CD8_CTL, Macro_IL1B, and Macro_LYVE1 were more abundant in Middle-aged or Old groups. These populations exhibited diverse pathway signatures related to inflammation, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. In addition, basal, club, and hillock cells exhibited higher scores for EMT-related transcriptional features and features associated with ECM remodeling in Old Hsa and Old Mmu groups. Fibro_IL1R1, Fibro_C7, and SMC_CNN1 were more abundant in Old Hsa and Old Mmu groups, with higher activity of pathways related to inflammation and ECM remodeling. Tip endothelial cells were more abundant in Old Hsa and Old Mmu groups, with higher angiogenesis-related pathway activity, whereas venous endothelial cells had higher activity of pathways related to inflammation and ECM remodeling. In summary, our study characterizes remodeling features of the immune microenvironment and tissue architecture associated with prostate aging and BPH across species.

title: Probiotic-based sequential delivery system for gut-brain co-therapy against inflammatory bowel disease-associated anxiety/depression.
abstract: NA: With the emergence of the gut-brain axis, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is no longer simply regarded as a localized intestinal disease but as a systemic disorder intimately associated with psychiatric comorbidities, including anxiety and depression. However, conventional therapeutic strategies predominantly target localized colonic inflammation, which often yields suboptimal outcomes. This highlights a critical need for gut-brain co-therapy to achieve comprehensive IBD management. Based on our observation that indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) possesses the potential to attenuate hippocampal neuroinflammation and subsequently modulate intestinal inflammation via the acetylcholine pathway, we engineered a gut-brain co-therapy delivery platform (CB-ASA/IAA/L). This system comprises Clostridium butyricum (CB) loaded with 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), encapsulated by a pH-responsive Eudragit L100-55 layer incorporating IAA. This microecological preparation is based on effective protection and delivery of CB, achieving the delivery of IAA to the brain and 5-ASA to the colon simultaneously. This sequential-release delivery system achieved intestinal barrier repair, promoted macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype, and restored Th17/Treg balance to recover intestinal homeostasis, while simultaneously alleviating anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in colitis mice. Importantly, the system demonstrated a robust ability to prevent inflammatory recurrence, a major clinical challenge in IBD treatment. This research offers a new avenue for the effective treatment of IBD-associated anxiety/depression by coordinating neuroimmune modulation with local intestinal repair.

title: Disrupting the interaction between T lymphocytes and microglia: Mechanism of Huanglian Jiedu Decoction in the treatment of ischemic stroke.
abstract: NA: Our previous studies have shown that Huanglian Jiedu Decoction effectively suppresses central immune-inflammatory responses, modulates peripheral inflammatory mediators, reduces the infiltration of peripheral T lymphocytes into the central nervous system, and promotes the conversion of infiltrated T lymphocytes in the brain into Treg cells. However, whether Huanglian Jiedu Decoction can influence M2 microglial polarization by regulating T-lymphocyte phenotypic transformation and thereby modulate neuroinflammation after ischemic stroke remains unclear. This study focused on Treg-mediated microglial polarization to investigate the potential of Huanglian Jiedu Decoction to modulate interactions between T lymphocytes and microglia in the treatment of ischemic stroke. We established a rat model of middle cerebral artery occlusion, an inflammatory model of Jurkat T cells stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate and ionomycin, and a Transwell co-culture model of T lymphocytes and HMC3 microglia. The results showed that Huanglian Jiedu Decoction effectively alleviated cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury in a rat model of middle cerebral artery, inhibited central inflammatory responses, and promoted the polarization of microglia toward the M2 phenotype. Huanglian Jiedu Decoction also promoted the conversion of CD4+ T cells in brain tissue into regulatory T cells and regulated regulatory T cells through the interleukin-10/Janus kinase 1/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 pathway, thereby promoting the activation of M2 microglia. These findings suggest that Huanglian Jiedu Decoction, which has heat-clearing and detoxifying properties, can regulate immune homeostasis, inhibit secondary neuroinflammation associated with ischemic stroke, and exert neuroprotective effects. Huanglian Jiedu Decoction may therefore treat ischemic stroke by modulating the interaction between T lymphocytes and microglia, providing a traditional Chinese medicine-based strategy for the treatment of ischemic stroke.

title: From broad suppression to precision targeting: the new era of antigen-specific immunotherapy for type 1 diabetes.
abstract: NA: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the selective destruction of pancreatic β-cells driven by autoreactive immune responses. In recent decades, the global incidence of T1D has risen markedly, with the most rapid increase observed among children and adolescents, imposing a substantial burden on healthcare systems worldwide. Conventional treatment primarily relies on exogenous insulin administration, which manages hyperglycemia but does not address the underlying autoimmune pathology or restore endogenous insulin production. Antigen-specific immunotherapy (ASI) has emerged as a promising strategy that may restore antigen-specific immune tolerance via multiple mechanisms, including clonal deletion/ anergy, immune deviation, induction of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and type 1 regulatory T (Tr1) cells, and tolerogenic antigen presentation. ASI may help preserve residual β-cell function and potentially modify disease progression. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in ASI for T1D, with a focus on the biological features of key T1D autoantigens, optimization of antigen delivery strategies, and prospects for clinical translation.

title: Immune Mechanisms of Oral Tolerance in the Prevention of IgE-Mediated Food Allergy.
abstract: NA: IgE-mediated food allergy develops when the immune response to dietary antigens is diverted from active tolerance towards a pathogenic type 2 immune response. Oral tolerance is the default, antigen-specific suppression of immune responses to ingested proteins. Early introduction trials, most notably the LEAP study, have demonstrated that oral exposure to food antigens during the first year of life can prevent food allergy and generate durable tolerance. Mechanistic advances have revealed that oral tolerance is governed by the coordinated activity of multiple overlapping immune layers. These include transcellular antigen transport through goblet cell-associated antigen passages (GAPs), tolerogenic antigen presentation by specialized RORγt+ antigen presenting cells (APCs) and classical dendritic cells (cDCs), induction and maintenance of heterogeneous regulatory T cell programs, and germinal center regulation of IgE and IgG responses. These cellular programs are further modulated by genetic determinants including HLA class II alleles, filaggrin variants, and microbial metabolites such as butyrate and indole derivatives and non-allergic dietary components. Infections can break tolerance by displacing or reprogramming tolerogenic APCs. Once food allergy has been established, regulatory pathways generated by oral allergen exposure are not sufficient to establish tolerance. These findings support a model in which tolerance and allergy represent competing, self-reinforcing immune states stabilized by redundant regulatory circuits. This review synthesizes the current understanding of these multilayered mechanisms and discusses their implications for prevention and treatment of food allergy.
journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology

title: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab in surgically resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (PRIME-HCC): a prospective, phase 1b, single-arm trial and translational analyses.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab improves survival in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. We evaluated this combination as neoadjuvant therapy and investigated its effect on peripheral immunity and the tumour microenvironment.
METHODS: PRIME-HCC is a single-arm, phase 1b trial in adults (aged ≥18 years) with early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, Child-Pugh A liver function, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1. Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg intravenously on days 1 and 22 of the first and second cycle) and ipilimumab (1 mg/kg intravenously on day 1 of the first cycle only) before liver resection. The primary endpoint was safety, assessed by treatment-related delays to surgery and adverse events in the intention-to-treat population. Translational analyses included imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics on paired tumour samples, peripheral immunophenotyping, T-cell receptor (TCR) β sequencing, and longitudinal tumour-agnostic circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) profiling. This trial was registered with EudraCT (2018-000987-27) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03682276); follow-up is currently ongoing.
FINDINGS: Between Sept 18, 2019, and Sept 28, 2023, of 43 patients assessed for eligibility, 33 patients were enrolled (25 [76%] male and 8 [24%] female; median age 68 years [range 38-80; IQR 63-73]); median follow-up was 25·7 months (95% CI 21·2-30·1). Any-grade adverse events occurred in 31 (94%) of patients, with treatment-related adverse events (trAEs) in 25 (76%) patients. Grade 3 trAEs occurred in three (9%) patients (transaminase elevation, anaemia, and dyspnoea). Serious adverse events were recorded in three (9%) patients, and no grade 4-5 events or treatment-related deaths occurred. 30 (91%) patients underwent surgery, including two (6%) who had immune checkpoint inhibitor-related surgical delays. Objective response rate by RECIST 1.1 was noted in eight (25%; 95% CI 13-42) patients (one complete response and seven partial responses), with 31 (97%; 84-100) patients achieving disease control. The absence of ctDNA after surgery was associated with improved 2-year recurrence-free survival (nine [82%] of 11 patients vs two [29%] of seven; p=0·049), as was at least 50% ctDNA reduction (median not reached [95% CI not reached] vs 20·9 months [95% CI 16·3-25·4]; HR 0·14 [95% CI 0·02-0·91]; p=0·039). Patients with objective responses showed expansion of peripheral PD-1-positive, Ki-67-positive, CD8-positive T cells (T-responding exhausted cells [Tresp]), associated with higher baseline intratumoral progenitor-exhausted T cells (Tpex) and increased Tresp infiltration. Patients whose disease did not respond to treatment exhibited enrichment of terminally exhausted CD8-positive T cells (Tex-term; CD8-positive PD-1-positive TOX-positive cells) and regulatory T cells.
INTERPRETATION: Neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab is feasible in early-stage resectable hepatocellular carcinoma, and later-phase randomised trials are needed to confirm the efficacy of this treatment strategy. Longitudinal ctDNA monitoring could support detection of minimal residual disease and warrants further prospective validation.
FUNDING: Bristol Myers Squibb, Cancer Research UK, Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro, and Foundation for Liver Research.

title: Acid-triggered carboxymethyl chitosan-stabilized synchronously mineralized collagen modified implants: Osteoimmunity regulation of bone defect repair in osteoporosis.
abstract: NA: Carboxymethyl chitosan (CMC)-stabilized amorphous strontium carbonate was integrated into synchronously mineralized collagen and covalently immobilized on polyetheretherketone (PEEK) to construct an acid-responsive osteoimmunomodulatory interface (GP-SSMC) for osteoporotic bone repair. In the acidic osteoporotic microenvironment, the protonation of carboxyl groups on CMC molecules accelerated Sr2+ release in situ while enabling adaptive modulation of interfacial properties. This response reprogrammed macrophages toward a c-Maf-associated M2 phenotype, increased IL-10 production, suppressed osteoclastogenesis, and shifted the TH17/Treg balance toward a regenerative immune state. GP-SSMC also promoted osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs and enhanced peri-implant bone formation in vivo. In an osteoporotic rabbit femoral defect model, GP-SSMC increased BV/TV by 97.3% compared with unmodified PEEK at 8 weeks. These findings demonstrate that a CMC-directed synchronously mineralized collagen interface can translate pathological acidity into adaptive Sr2+ delivery and coordinated osteoimmune regulation, providing a promising strategy for osseointegration in osteoporotic bone defects.

title: An Ii-Key-containing HPV16/18 E7 epitope peptide vaccine promotes dendritic cell activation and T-cell immunity in a murine HPV16 tumor model, with greater tumor control upon PD-1 blockade.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Therapeutic vaccines targeting human papillomavirus (HPV) E6/E7 oncoproteins represent a promising strategy for cervical cancer immunotherapy, yet most candidates remain constrained by insufficient antigen presentation efficiency and suboptimal T-cell responses. The Ii-Key strategy, which links the invariant chain (Ii) core motif to epitope peptides to facilitate MHC class II loading, may overcome this limitation by amplifying CD4+ T helper responses.
METHODS: HPV16/18 E7 epitopes restricted by murine H-2 class I/II molecules were predicted using immunoinformatics tools. Ii-Key-modified MHC class II peptides (LRMK-PEG2-epitope) and unmodified MHC class I peptides were synthesized and evaluated in vitro using bone marrow-derived dendritic cell (BMDC) stimulation assays with flow cytometry, ELISA, and western blotting. In vivo immunogenicity was assessed in C57BL/6 mice through immune phenotyping of lymphoid organs and plasma cytokine profiling. Anti-tumor activity was tested in an early-intervention subcutaneous TC-1 tumor model (HPV16 E6/E7-positive) with histopathological and flow cytometric analyses of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. Combination treatment with anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody was also examined.
RESULTS: The peptide pool promoted BMDC maturation, as evidenced by increased frequencies of CD80+CD86+ and I-A/I-E+ BMDCs, NF-κB pathway activation, and increased proinflammatory cytokine secretion; these readouts indicate DC activation. In C57BL/6 mice, peptide immunization induced DC activation in draining lymph nodes, enhanced CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation (CD8+ increase significant only in non-tumor-bearing mice), reduced Treg proportions in tumor-bearing mice (with a non-significant decline in non-tumor-bearing mice), elicited direct ex vivo splenocyte cytotoxicity against TC-1 cells, and altered memory-phenotype T-cell frequencies, increasing TCM frequency in non-tumor-bearing mice and TEM frequency in tumor-bearing mice. In the TC-1 model, peptide treatment suppressed tumor growth and qualitatively reduced tumor Ki67 staining, accompanied by non-significant trends toward increased intratumoral CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell frequencies. Combination with anti-PD-1 produced greater tumor control than either monotherapy. Safety assessments by histopathology and serum biochemistry indicated acceptable tolerability under the conditions and observation period tested.
CONCLUSIONS: The Ii-Key-containing HPV16/18 E7 peptide formulation promoted dendritic cell activation and T-cell immunity, achieving anti-tumor activity in an early-intervention TC-1 model with acceptable tolerability. The combination with PD-1 blockade produced greater tumor control than either monotherapy; this comparison does not establish additivity or synergy. These preclinical findings support further evaluation of the formulation incorporating direct antigen-presentation assays and matched unmodified MHC-II peptide controls.

title: Hyperinsulinemia contributes to regulatory T-cell dysfunction and disease activity in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: NA: We examined relationships among obesity, hyperinsulinemia, regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, and activity in multiple sclerosis (MS), and investigated insulin signaling as a candidate mechanism. We prospectively followed 131 patients with relapsing-remitting MS, stratified by body mass index, for at least 36 months. Clinical and MRI outcomes were assessed longitudinally, whereas metabolic parameters and Treg phenotype and function were evaluated at baseline. Mechanistic studies examined insulin receptor signaling in purified Tregs using insulin stimulation, pharmacological inhibition, insulin receptor silencing, and functional assays. In a separate, non-overlapping cohort, 28 obese hyperinsulinemic patients with relapsing-remitting MS underwent a 24-week metformin intervention with longitudinal metabolic and immunological assessments. Obese patients had higher fasting insulin, more relapses, disability progression, and MRI activity. Hyperinsulinemia correlated with reduced FoxP3 and IL-10, impaired Treg suppression, and increased IFN-γ and IL-17 in Treg-enriched cultures. Insulin stimulation altered AKT-mTOR signaling and Treg function; AKT inhibition or insulin receptor silencing reversed these effects. Obese-patient Tregs suppressed myelin-reactive responses less effectively. During metformin treatment, reductions in fasting insulin and AKT-mTOR signaling were accompanied by improvements in Treg phenotype and suppressive function and attenuation of myelin-specific inflammatory responses. These immunological changes correlated with insulin reductions, but the single-arm design and metformin's direct effects preclude causal attribution. These findings support an association between hyperinsulinemia, altered Treg function, and inflammatory disease activity in MS and identify insulin signaling as a candidate pathway for further mechanistic investigation.

title: ITK deficiency protects against autoimmune pulmonary hemorrhage in mice by promoting amphiregulin-producing regulatory T cells.
abstract: NA: Pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) is a life-threatening manifestation of systemic autoimmunity caused by immune-mediated disruption of the alveolar capillary barrier. Despite high mortality, the molecular checkpoints that shift destructive inflammation toward protective immune regulation remain poorly defined. Here, using a pristane-induced PH mouse model, we identify interleukin-2-inducible T-cell kinase (ITK) as a critical regulator of autoimmune lung injury. ITK deficiency (Itk⁻/⁻) conferred near-complete protection from PH and associated multiorgan injury, accompanied by reduced proinflammatory monocytes and neutrophils and increased Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs). Adoptive transfer of Itk⁻/⁻ Tregs protected wild-type recipients from PH and suppressed systemic proinflammatory cytokines, identifying Tregs as key mediators of tissue protection. Mechanistically, lung Itk⁻/⁻ Tregs exhibited increased amphiregulin, a mediator of tissue repair. Transcriptomic profiling further showed that ITK loss reprogrammed Tregs toward a metabolically and functionally enhanced state, with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, and STAT5 signaling, and tissue-repair programs. These findings establish ITK as a regulator of the balance between pulmonary injury and reparative immunity and support targeting the ITK axis in severe inflammatory lung disease.

title: Lactate-induced histone lactylation drives PRMT5-mediated Foxp3 symmetric dimethylation to promote Treg differentiation and sepsis immunopathology.
abstract: NA: Sepsis is characterized by persistent immune dysfunction but how metabolic alterations contribute to immunosuppression remains unclear. Here, we identify lactate as a regulator of regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation and show that Treg accumulation contributes to persistent organ injury during sepsis. In patients with sepsis, plasma lactate correlates with circulating Treg frequencies and disease severity. Lactate uptake through MCT1 increases H3K9 and H3K18 lactylation and Prmt5 transcription. Lactate also increases S-adenosylmethionine, supporting PRMT5-mediated symmetric dimethylation of Foxp3 at R51 and R146, which stabilizes Foxp3 and promotes Treg differentiation and suppressive function. CD4+ T cell-specific Prmt5 deletion attenuates lactate-induced Treg responses and improves outcomes in septic mice. Dexmedetomidine binds the PRMT5/MEP50 complex, reduces Treg accumulation and organ injury, and improves host defense against secondary infection. These findings link lactate metabolism to PRMT5-dependent Foxp3 stabilization and suggest a potential therapeutic pathway for sepsis-associated immunosuppression.

title: Spatial Immune Organization Associates with Response to CD40 Agonism in BCG-Unresponsive Non-Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer: A Phase I Trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: CD40 agonists activate dendritic cells (DCs) and promote T-cell antitumor immunity, but clinical development has been limited by systemic toxicity and incomplete understanding of determinants of response. In this phase I study (NCT05126472), we evaluated the safety, preliminary clinical activity, and spatial immune correlates of response to intravesical Fc-optimized CD40 agonist 2141-V11 in 25 patients with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG)-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients received weekly intravesical instillations for 3 weeks, with retreatment at weeks 13 and 25 based on disease status. Primary objectives were safety, tolerability, and determination of the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D). Secondary endpoints included pharmacokinetics and preliminary clinical activity. Exploratory endpoints including multiplex spatial profiling on tumor specimens to define correlates of response.
RESULTS: Intravesical 2141-V11 was well tolerated, and the MTD was not reached. The RP2D was established at 70 mg. Preliminary clinical activity was observed in 40% of patients, with a median response duration of 20 months. Clinical response was associated with distinct organization of tertiary lymphoid structures, characterized by the presence of DC-CXCL13+ CD4+ and CD8+ T cell triads. Following treatment, responders exhibited decreased proximity between DCs and regulatory T cells (Tregs), whereas non-responders exhibited increased DC-Treg proximity.
CONCLUSIONS: Intravesical 2141-V11 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and preliminary antitumor activity. Spatial profiling revealed immune-cell organizations associated with clinical response, identifying candidate biomarkers and potential strategies for therapeutic combinations. These findings support further clinical evaluation of intravesical 2141-V11 in phase II studies.
journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research

title: Continuous in situ production of CAR T cells from in vivo-transduced HSCs is safe and delays growth of mouse HER2high tumors.
abstract: NA: Clinical trials with CAR T cells for solid tumors have suggested a number of problems, including critical autoimmune reactions caused by high-affinity CAR T cells, development of CAR T cell exhaustion, poor trafficking to tumor sites after intravenous CAR T cell injection, and high costs. To address these problems, we tested an in vivo HSC gene therapy approach, resulting in in situ production of low-affinity mHER2-CAR-expressing T-cells in physiologically relevant immunocompetent mouse models with tumors derived from mouse HER2high tumor cell lines, KPmHER2 and B16F10mHER2. After intravenous injection of integrating helper-dependent adenovirus (HDAd) vectors expressing mHER2-CAR under T cell restricted transcriptional and miRNA control into mobilized C57BL/6-based mice and in vivo enrichment of stably transduced HSCs, we demonstrated that mHER2-CAR T cells significantly delayed tumor growth. Additional Treg depletion by systemic administration of low-dose cyclophosphamide further extended the time of tumor relapse driven by mHER2-negative cells. Despite continuous mHER2-CAR T cell production, the in vivo approach had an excellent safety profile. Our study also revealed a number of obstacles that limit the efficacy of the in vivo approach and have to be addressed in the future.

title: Regulatory T cell therapy and immune tolerance in heart transplantation: a translational evidence framework for regulatory T cells-cell characterization and recipient-graft monitoring.
abstract: NA: Regulatory T cell (Treg) therapy is a candidate strategy for improving donor-specific immune regulation after heart transplantation and, in the long term, may reduce reliance on lifelong immunosuppression. This Review separates mechanistic and preclinical evidence from human case observations, prospective clinical-trial protocols, manufacturing studies, and translational hypotheses. We summarize pathways that support Treg function in experimental transplantation and evaluate context-dependent outputs, including amphiregulin and CXCL15-related signaling, as potential safety signals rather than validated clinical biomarkers. We then compare peripheral-blood-derived and thymus-derived Treg-cell preparations, focusing on source material, manufacturing, cryopreservation, cell identity and potency, and infusion timing. Human evidence for Thy-Tregs in heart transplantation includes one fully reported index case and preliminary, incompletely reported data on the first four THYTECH recipients. ATT-Heart provides a prospective phase I evaluation framework. Finally, we assess allogeneic Thy-Treg banks, thymic organoids, and thymic transplantation as exploratory routes for adult recipients. The central translational question is whether a defined Treg-cell therapy can persist, remain functionally stable, and be monitored safely in the inflammatory environment of cardiac transplantation.

title: Lactylation-mediated remodeling of spatial immunometabolic niches in lung cancer: metabolic origins, cellular interactions, and molecular mechanisms.
abstract: NA: Hypoxia, abnormal perfusion, and oncogenic signaling increase lactate production in lung cancer and create intercellular fluxes mediated by monocarboxylate transporters. Circulating lactate can be taken up by lung tumors and enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Lactate therefore acts as a carbon source, a regulator of redox and acid-base homeostasis, and a precursor for lysine L-lactylation. Representative validated modifications include histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la) and histone H4 lysine 5 lactylation (H4K5la) together with nonhistone substrates such as programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), hexokinase 2 (HK2), mitochondrial cristae-organizing protein Mic60, and replication protein A1 (RPA1), linking lactylation to transcriptional regulation, protein stability, metabolic adaptation, immune evasion, DNA repair, and treatment resistance in lung cancer. Tumor-derived lactate also reprograms cluster of differentiation 8-positive (CD8+) T cells, regulatory T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and cancer-associated fibroblasts across hypoxic cores, invasive fronts, perivascular regions, and tertiary lymphoid structure-associated areas. This review integrates lactate-pool formation, lactylation writers and erasers, intracellular reprogramming, immune-stromal interactions, and spatial niches. It distinguishes metabolic and acidification effects of lactate from covalent lactylation and separates direct causal evidence in lung cancer from spatial associations and cross-cancer mechanistic support. This framework defines a source-to-site chain for studying regional lactate activity and lactylation-dependent phenotypes in lung cancer.

title: Safeguarding functionality of ATMPs: in-depth characterization of cryopreserved GMP-compliant nTreg products for therapeutic use.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Regulatory T cell (Treg) therapy has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for restoring immune tolerance. However, its broader clinical implementation requires cryopreservation strategies that reliably preserve the biological integrity of therapeutic Treg products during Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) manufacturing. The feasibility of reduced dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) cryopreservation, including in our previous study, has been demonstrated. Yet its effects on the functional, metabolic, epigenetic, and molecular characteristics of therapeutic natural Treg (nTreg) products remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated the biological responses of GMP-compliant nTreg products to cryopreservation and determined whether reducing DMSO from 10% to 5% preserves key product characteristics after thawing.
METHODS: Human GMP-compliant CD4+CD25+FOXP3+ nTreg products were cryopreserved using serum- and xeno-free formulations containing DMSO at different concentration. Fresh and cryopreserved cells were evaluated immediately (0 h) and 24 h after thawing by integrated viability, phenotypic, functional, metabolic, FOXP3 Treg-specific demethylation region (TSDR) analysis, and single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility analyses.
RESULTS: High-resolution respirometry demonstrated a transient mitochondrial activation following cryopreservation, while TSDR analysis confirmed maintenance of epigenetic lineage identity. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling revealed modest, donor-dependent responses to cryopreservation, with no significant differentially expressed genes between the 10% and 5% DMSO conditions under the predefined criteria. Single-cell chromatin-accessibility analysis showed broadly comparable accessibility-defined population architecture and preservation of accessibility at the assessed Treg lineage-associated loci FOXP3, IKZF2, and IL2RA. Reduction of DMSO to 5% in cryopreservation attenuated delayed cellular impairment, while maintaining phenotypic purity, cytokine quiescence, suppressive function, TSDR status, and high viability across 0 h and 24 h after thawing.
CONCLUSION: This study provides biological insight into the cellular responses of therapeutic Tregs to cryopreservation, while demonstrating that reduced DMSO cryopreservation preserves the investigated phenotypic, functional and molecular charactersitics of GMP-compliant nTreg products. By minimizing cryopreservation-associated cellular stress and reducing DMSO exposure to patients, this study supports the clincial applicability of reduced-DMSO cryopreservation within the investigated GMP manufacturing workflow, and may facilitate future implementation of cryopreserved Treg products by providing greater flexibility for product release, storage, and distribution.
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

title: Immune and environmental determinants of diabetic bone fragility: bone microenvironment remodeling, organ crosstalk, and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: NA: Diabetic bone disease is increasingly recognized as a complication in which fracture risk exceeds what bone mineral density (BMD) predicts: in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) despite preserved or elevated BMD, and in type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) beyond its BMD deficit. We re-examine this problem through the immune-metabolic axis, using the gut-bone axis as an organizing framework that links the bone microenvironment to multi-organ communication, and we assign every mechanistic claim an explicit evidence level. Gut dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability and loss of microbial metabolites are treated as candidate upstream amplifiers rather than established drivers: hyperglycemia-induced barrier failure and metabolic endotoxemia are documented in diabetes, whereas the short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-regulatory T cell-WNT10B pathway and gut-to-marrow T-cell trafficking have been shown principally in non-diabetic rodents, and no longitudinal or interventional study has yet linked diabetes-associated dysbiosis to a skeletal endpoint. We summarize how advanced glycation end products (AGEs), oxidative stress, NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling, AMPK-mTOR imbalance and epigenetic memory suppress bone formation while priming osteoclastogenic signaling, and we propose a stage- and context-dependent model of remodeling uncoupling that reconciles this signaling with the low bone turnover measured in human T2DM. The osteoimmune niche is then considered across four compartments: primed macrophage-osteoclast signaling, Th17/Treg disequilibrium, stromal-cell fate shift with marrow adiposity, and osteocyte dysfunction. We set out the diabetes-specific molecular alterations of the gut-bone axis, including GLUT2-dependent barrier failure, convergence of lipopolysaccharide-TLR4 and AGE-RAGE signaling on NF-κB, and loss of SCFA-GPR43/GPR109A signaling. Environmental and systemic determinants, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and stage-dependent chronic kidney disease, are integrated with five bone-organ axes (pancreas, gut, adipose, liver, kidney) to show how skeletal injury becomes embedded in multi-organ inflammation. Therapeutic directions are grounded in clinical evidence and safety: licensed antiresorptive agents retain their efficacy in T2DM, whereas microbiota-directed, immune-cell and epigenetic strategies remain experimental. Framing diabetic bone disease as evidence-graded osteoimmune remodeling, with dysbiosis treated as a candidate amplifier, may refine risk assessment, biomarker development and the design of trials that test combination hypotheses.

title: Targeting the Lactate-Lactylation Axis in Cancer Immunotherapy Resistance: From Tumor Acidosis to Context-Dependent Immune Reprogramming.
abstract: NA: Lactate is now recognized as an active immunometabolic regulator in the tumor microenvironment (TME), not simply as a glycolytic byproduct. Its immunological effects arise through several related but distinct routes. Extracellular acidosis, glucose competition, and impaired monocarboxylate transporter-dependent flux can impair CD8+ T cells, natural killer cells, and dendritic cells. Lactate- and proton-sensing receptors can also favor suppressive myeloid and regulatory-cell programs. Histone and non-histone lactylation add another layer by linking lactate availability to chromatin regulation and protein function. During sustained or repeated metabolic stress, these processes may support regulatory T-cell fitness, suppressive programs in tumor-associated macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, checkpoint expression, and resistance to immunotherapy. Lactylation is a plausible mediator through which sustained metabolic stress may be converted into persistent immune reprogramming; however, post-withdrawal persistence and cellular memory remain to be demonstrated in cancer. We distinguish lactate-dependent regulation from acidosis and evaluate the links to immune dysfunction and treatment resistance by their temporal, causal, and clinical support. This framework defines tests of post-exposure persistence and connects mechanistic evidence and pharmacological specificity to biomarker development and mechanism-matched trial design.

title: Immune potentiating effects of the HDAC inhibitor Zabadinostat on human immune and tumor cells.
abstract: NA: The use of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACis) to reverse epigenetic silencing of immune-associated genes has shown clinical efficacy in hematologic malignancies but not solid tumors. Here we explored the transcriptional and phenotypic effects of in vitro exposures of Zabadinostat, a second-generation class I HDACi, on human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and solid tumor cells to support its combination with immunotherapy. Zabadinostat induced activation of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells and natural killer cells, while reducing the frequency and suppressive function of regulatory T cells. Increases in stem-like memory T cells, a rare subset of multipotent, self-renewing cells important for anti-tumor control, were also observed, and these immune effects coincided with increased expression of transcriptional activation marks H3K9ac and H3K27ac. Zabadinostat increased PD-L1, FAS, ICAM-1, and HLA expression in tumor cells and reverted epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related proteins. These data show that Zabadinostat is a novel immunomodulatory agent with multifaceted effects, capable of enhancing immune effector function, reducing immunosuppression, and improving the visibility of tumor cells to immune-mediated attack. These findings support the use of Zabadinostat in combination with immunotherapeutic agents.

title: Dual-Targeted Thalidomide Nanoliposomes Suppress Neutrophil-Driven Inflammation in Intestinal Behçet's Disease.
abstract: NA: Excessive neutrophil recruitment, vascular activation, and platelet-associated inflammatory interfaces are implicated in intestinal tissue injury in intestinal Behçet's disease (intestinal BD), whereas conventional systemic therapies offer limited spatial control over drug exposure within active intestinal lesions. Here, we developed thalidomide-loaded nanoliposomes co-functionalized with a neutrophil elastase-binding peptide (NEBP) and a P-selectin-binding peptide (PSN), designated Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip, to engage complementary activated neutrophil-associated and P-selectin-associated inflammatory interfaces. Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 116.6 ± 5.7 nm, a thalidomide encapsulation efficiency of 91.43 ± 0.71%, and reduced initial burst release, while maintaining colloidal stability during storage and simulated gastrointestinal exposure. Surface ligand density was estimated from the feed composition. Ligand-dependent interactions were observed in activated endothelial cells and neutrophil-like cells; in activated endothelial cells, liposome-associated fluorescence increased from 7.42% for Thd-Lip to 40.55% for Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip and decreased to 1.10% following free PSN competition. Additional validation supported PSN-dependent association with activated platelets and greater inflamed-tissue association of the dual-ligand formulation than with either single-ligand formulation. In vivo, Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip showed preferential and prolonged retention within inflamed intestinal tissues, with intestinal fluorescence remaining approximately 2.6-fold higher than that of Thd-Lip at 24 h. LC-MS/MS quantification further showed increased total intestinal thalidomide exposure and a higher intestine/plasma concentration ratio after Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip administration. In a murine intestinal BD-like model, Thd-NEBP/PSN-Lip alleviated intestinal injury, restored colon length toward the healthy level, reduced neutrophil infiltration and local inflammatory cytokine expression, attenuated responses involving IL-17A+CD4+ and IFN-γ+CD4+ T cells, and partially restored the Foxp3+ regulatory T cell compartment. Microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses further indicated broader treatment-associated changes in the intestinal inflammatory microenvironment. Collectively, these findings suggest that dual-targeted nanoliposomes improve lesion-directed thalidomide delivery and suppress neutrophil-driven intestinal inflammation, supporting a pathology-guided nanotherapeutic strategy for intestinal BD.

title: Paeoniflorin Modulates Gut Microbiota-Derived Lysophospholipids to Restore Th17/Treg Homeostasis in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by dysregulated immune responses. Paeoniflorin (PF), a highly purified monoterpene glycoside derived from Paeonia lactiflora, exhibits immunomodulatory activity, but its mechanisms in SLE remain unclear. This study investigated whether PF ameliorates SLE by modulating the gut microbiota-lipid metabolite axis and restoring Th17/Treg immune balance.
METHODS: Network pharmacology was applied to predict PF-related targets and pathways in SLE. MRL/lpr mice were treated with PF, and disease severity was assessed by clinical manifestations, autoantibody levels, renal function, and histopathology. Intestinal barrier integrity and motility were evaluated in vivo. Th17 and Treg cell populations in intestinal and peripheral immune tissues were analyzed by flow cytometry. Gut microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and untargeted LC-MS/MS-based metabolomics of intestinal contents was performed to identify differential metabolites and enriched metabolic pathways.
RESULTS: PF treatment significantly alleviated lupus-like manifestations in MRL/lpr mice, including reduced splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, decreased serum anti-dsDNA, ANA, total IgG, and IL-17 levels, and improved renal function and histopathological injury. PF restored Th17/Treg balance by suppressing IL-17-producing CD4⁺ T cells and promoting Foxp3⁺ Treg cells across intestinal and peripheral immune compartments. PF also improved intestinal barrier integrity and reshaped gut microbial composition by reducing inflammation-associated taxa and enriching beneficial bacteria. Metabolomic analysis demonstrated that PF markedly downregulated glycerophospholipid metabolism, particularly reducing lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) and lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), which have been reported to promote RORγt activity and Th17 differentiation. Correlation analyses linked microbial alterations with lipid metabolite changes and Th17/Treg-associated immune parameters.
CONCLUSION: Paeoniflorin alleviates SLE by regulating a gut microbiota-lipid metabolite-immune axis, suppressing pro-Th17 lysophospholipid metabolism and restoring Th17/Treg immune homeostasis.

title: Structure-informed immunomodulation: how polysaccharides modulate selected components of the tumour immune microenvironment.
abstract: NA: Polysaccharides from fungi, plants and algae have been adjunctive cancer immunotherapies for decades, yet clinical impact lags the preclinical literature. This review treats them as structure-informed modulators of selected components of the tumour immune microenvironment, not as nonspecific biological response modifiers. We organize the evidence as one causal chain: fine structure influences which pattern-recognition receptor is engaged, receptor engagement shapes a signalling programme, and that programme shapes effector output; most preparations engage more than one receptor, so a response reflects their combined signalling. We advance three arguments. First, immunomodulation can be bidirectional: TLR4-NF-κB reportedly drives activating and suppressive outputs depending on structure, dose and tissue context, though suppressive outputs are documented only outside tumour models. Second, the most consequential recent evidence concerns relief of immunosuppression: PD-L1 downregulation, depletion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells, interference with regulatory T cells and the IL-35 axis, and sensitisation to checkpoint blockade. Third, translational failure reflects addressable barriers: batch heterogeneity, absent receptor-specific genetics, and no quantitative structure-activity model. Clinical evidence - two long-approved fungal preparations and one small single-arm trial - establishes feasibility, not efficacy; plant- and algal-derived polysaccharides remain preclinical or clinically preliminary. Conformational analytics, machine-learning-assisted modelling and engineered delivery may address them.

title: Short-chain fatty acids as tumor microenvironment modulators: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: NA: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are microbial metabolites generated through the fermentation of microbiota-accessible carbohydrates (MACs), including dietary fiber, resistant starch, resistant dextrins, non-digestible oligosaccharides, and other fermentable substrates. SCFAs can modulate tumor cell metabolism and the tumor microenvironment (TME), with reported effects on glycolysis, lipid biosynthesis, and oxidative phosphorylation that vary according to SCFA and cellular context. Simultaneously, they modulate innate and adaptive immunity, potentially enhancing cytotoxic T lymphocyte and NK cell function while also promoting regulatory T-cell responses and myeloid-derived suppressor cell activity under certain conditions. Epigenetically, SCFAs can inhibit histone deacetylases and modulate non-coding RNA networks, including changes in the expression of oncogenic and tumor-suppressive microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). These three axes-metabolic, immune, and epigenetic-converge to reshape the TME, but their net effects vary with SCFA identity, concentration, tumor type, and local microenvironmental cues, and may be either tumor-suppressive or tumor-promoting. Although preclinical studies support the therapeutic potential of SCFA modulation, rapid metabolism and poor bioavailability limit systemic application, while clinical evidence for direct antitumor efficacy remains limited. Key unanswered questions include which cancer profiles are most responsive, whether SCFAs may induce unintended immunological effects, and how targeted delivery systems might enhance therapeutic utility. In this review, we survey the biology and therapeutic potential of SCFAs within the TME, highlighting their context-dependent effects and the challenges that must be addressed before clinical translation.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease

title: Spatial and transcriptomic analyses reveal the adverse prognostic impact of regulatory T cells in follicular lymphoma treated with rituximab-lenalidomide.
abstract: NA: The prognostic impact of the tumour microenvironment in follicular lymphoma (FL) remains controversial. To adress this, we analysed FL samples from patients enrolled in the rituximab lenalidomide versus any chemotherapy (RELEVANCE) trial using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) and multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). RNA-seq analysis (n = 354) showed that regulatory T-cell (Treg) signatures were associated with shorter PFS in the whole cohort (HR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.01-2.41, p = 0.044), particularly in patients treated with rituximab-lenalidomide (LEN) (R2, HR= 1.84, 95% CI: 1-3.37, p = 0.046) but not with rituximab-chemotherapy (R-chemo, HR = 1.33, 95% CI: 0.71-2.48, p = 0.365). mIF analysis on tissue microarrays (TMA) (n = 394) showed that high infiltration of CD3+/CD4+/FOXP3+ Tregs was associated with shorter PFS in the overall cohort (HR = 1.951, CI: 1.259-3.024, p = 0.0023 log-rank test), particularly in the R2 arm (HR = 2.3, CI: 1.2-4.5, p = 0.0097 log-rank test) and remained significant after FL-International Prognostic Index (FLIPI) adjustment (HR = 1.843; 95% CI: 1.1-2.8, p = 0.006). Whole-slide mIF (WSI) performed in 64 selected cases confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of Tregs in R2-treated patients and further showed that extra-follicular Treg localization was specifically associated with shorter PFS (HR = 2.87, 95% CI: 1.13-7.28, p = 0.020). These data suggest that high Treg infiltration by mIF is associated with inferior outcome in lenalidomide-treated FL patients and may have potential value for risk stratification.

title: Gamma-delta T cells in neuroblastoma: Exploiting MHC-independent recognition to overcome the barriers of high-risk disease.
abstract: NA: Neuroblastoma is the most frequent extracranial solid tumor in children and the main cause of early childhood cancer deaths. Relapse occurs in more than half of high-risk patients despite rigorous multimodal therapy, and four-year overall survival in relapsed disease is approximately 20%. Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies and GD2-directed CAR T cell treatment have advanced the field, although neither has eliminated neuroblastoma's immune resistance. Current immunotherapy has three interrelated challenges. GD2 heterogeneity lets antigen-negative subclones escape and cause recurrence. Inhibitory cytokines, regulatory T cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells dominate the TME. MHC class I downregulation frequently renders traditional αβ T cell methods ineffective, even with the target antigen present. Gamma-delta (γδ) T cells offer a distinct mechanism. They recognize tumor targets without antigen presentation by sensing stress-induced ligands through NKG2D and DNAM-1 and phosphoantigens through butyrophilin proteins BTN3A1 and BTN2A1. This recognition holds regardless of MHC class I status. In conjunction with anti-GD2 antibodies, CD16 expression boosts antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In neuroblastoma lesions, γδ T cells are the primary antitumoral fraction in tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte products, indicating compatibility with the disease's immune system. This study examines neuroblastoma immunotherapy failure mechanisms and innovative γδ T cell platforms, such as non-engineered allogeneic products, composite γδ T plus NK cell techniques, and CAR- and AbTCR-modified designs. A biomarker-driven patient selection paradigm and product standardization, in vivo persistence, and TME suppression are examined. NCT05400603, the first trial of adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded allogeneic γδ T cells in a population that includes pediatric neuroblastoma patients, is crucial for proving the mechanism.

title: Histopathological and Transcriptomic Features of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-related T-cell-mediated Rejection in Liver Transplantation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related T-cell-mediated rejection (irTCMR) leads to greater steroid resistance and graft loss compared with conventional T-cell-mediated rejection (cTCMR) in liver transplant recipients. However, their histopathological and transcriptomic features remain poorly understood.
METHODS: Thirty-one adult recipients with biopsy-proven T-cell-mediated rejection (12 irTCMR and 19 cTCMR) were enrolled. Biopsies were assessed using the Banff and Ishak scoring systems, with immunohistochemical staining for CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, programmed death-ligand 1, and C4d. Spatial transcriptomic analysis was performed on the CD45-enriched portal areas.
RESULTS: irTCMR showed higher alanine aminotransferase/aspartate aminotransferase peaks, steroid-resistant rejection (33.3% versus 0%; P = 0.016), and graft loss (41.7% versus 0%; P = 0.005). IrTCMR had a higher rejection activity index (median 6 versus 5; P = 0.020), driven by more severe bile duct inflammation and venous endothelialitis. Ishak scoring revealed a higher histological activity index with greater confluent necrosis (P = 0.046). Both groups showed CD8+ predominant T-cell aggregates with sparse CD20+ B cells; CD4+ abundance (P = 0.079) and the CD4/CD8 ratio (P = 0.096) tended to be higher in irTCMR. Portal C4d deposition and programmed death-ligand 1 expression showed no significant differences. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct transcriptomic profiles in irTCMR, with 75 differentially expressed genes and enrichment of allograft rejection and antigen processing pathways. Immune deconvolution demonstrated increased CD4+ T cells, dendritic cells, and M1 macrophages but reduced regulatory T cells in irTCMR.
CONCLUSIONS: irTCMR is a distinct aggressive rejection phenotype with severe bile duct inflammation, venous endothelialitis, confluent necrosis, and transcriptomic features distinct from cTCMR. These features underscore the need for further research on the pathogenesis of irTCMR.

title: Causal Associations of Perturbational Phenotyping of Human Blood Cells and CHB: a Mendelian Randomization Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The dynamic interaction between the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and the host's inflammatory response plays a key role in determining the extent of hepatic injury and disease progression. This study aimed to elucidate the causal relationships among perturbational phenotypes of human blood cells, immune cell dynamics, and chronic hepatitis B infection (CHB) and to further validate these immune traits at the single-cell transcriptional level.
METHODS: This study systematically summarized genome-wide association studies (GWAS) investigating 91 perturbational phenotypes of human blood cells in relation to CHB. Furthermore, a mediator Mendelian randomization analysis was performed to assess the potential mediating roles of immune cells in the causal framework linking perturbational phenotypes of human blood cells to CHB. To validate key MR-derived immune features, single-cell RNA-seq data from CHB patients and healthy controls were analyzed to delineate immune cell populations and characterize cell-state alterations.
RESULTS: The analysis identified one perturbational phenotype of human blood cells that showed a causal association with CHB in individuals of European ancestry. This phenotype involved the eosinophil perturbation response, represented by the side scatter median of eosinophil 1 at baseline, measured using WDF dye. The findings suggest that this response mediates CHB risk through CD33 expressed on CD33br HLA-DR+ CD14dim cells. Two additional perturbational phenotypes of human blood cells were causally related to CHB: neutrophil perturbation response (neutrophil 2/neutrophil 4 ratio in response to water perturbation measured by WDF dye) and platelet perturbation response (side scatter standard deviation of platelets in response to captopril perturbation measured by WNR dye). The neutrophil perturbation response influenced CHB risk through Mo MDSC AC, HLA-DR on CD14+ CD16- monocytes, and HLA-DR on CD14+ monocytes. The platelet perturbation response mediated CHB risk through Sw mem%B cells, secreting Treg %CD4 cells, CD25++ CD8br %T cells, and CD28+ CD45RA- CD8br %CD8br cells. Single-cell RNA-seq analysis further confirmed these MR findings by showing expanded inflammatory monocytes and MDSC-like cells, increased cytotoxic and regulatory T-cell activity, and reduced switched memory B-cell signatures in CHB.
CONCLUSIONS: This study provides genetic evidence supporting a potential causal relationship between perturbational phenotypes of human blood cells and CHB, indicating that immune cells may act as intermediaries in mediating this association. The integration of MR and single-cell profiling strengthens the biological plausibility of these pathways and highlights key immune states involved in HBV persistence and disease progression.

title: Early Inflammatory Biomarkers and Outcomes After Liver Transplantation: A pilot Single-Center Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Early allograft dysfunction (EAD) and ischemic-type biliary lesions (ITBL) remain significant complications following liver transplantation, with limited understanding of their pathogenesis and opportunities for prevention. This exploratory pilot study investigated the associations of perioperative cytokine profiles with EAD, ITBL and other long-term complications.
METHODS: In this prospective observational study, 33 patients undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation between February and November 2023 were enrolled. Two patients required re-transplantation, resulting in 35 procedures analyzed. Blood samples were collected preoperatively, at 4 hours post-reperfusion, and on postoperative days 1, 4, 7, and 30±4. Cytokine profiles were analyzed using Luminex multiplex assays, and immune cell populations characterized by flow cytometry. The associations between these immunological measurements and clinical outcomes were systematically evaluated.
RESULTS: EAD developed in 57% (20/35) of transplantations. Interleukin-1α (IL-1α) levels at 4 hours after reperfusion were significantly elevated in EAD patients (median 9.6 vs 0.8 pg/mL, p=0.005) with an AUROC of 0.82. Additional pro-inflammatory mediators including Macrophage Migration Inhibitory Factor (MIF), IL-16, and IL-17 also showed significant associations with EAD development. The IL-1α/IL-1RA ratio was associated with subsequent ITBL development (AUROC 0.80). Hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) levels were elevated in patients with biliary complications. Chemokines Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1 (MCP-1) and Stromal Cell-Derived Factor-1α (SDF-1α) at POD1 were similarly associated with subsequent ITBL development. Last, patients with EAD showed reduced fractions of CD4+ T cells and regulatory T cells in blood samples.
CONCLUSIONS: Early postoperative IL-1α elevation was associated with subsequent EAD development following liver transplantation. MIF, IL-16, and IL-17 provide additional discriminatory power. The preoperative IL-1α/IL-1RA ratio and postoperative HGF, MCP-1, and SDF-1α levels were associated with ITBL development. These biomarkers may help identify patients at risk and warrant validation in larger cohorts to confirm these results and explore their potential to guide therapeutic interventions in the critical early post-transplant period.
journal: European surgical research. Europaische chirurgische Forschung. Recherches chirurgicales europeennes

title: The Phosphatidylinositol-3-Kinase δ-Isoform Instructs Differentiation of Regulatory T-Lymphocytes in the Thymus.
abstract: NA: Regulatory T cells (Treg) are essential actors in the establishment and maintenance of immune tolerance to self and innocuous non-self. A functionally heterogeneous Treg population develops in the thymus, but the molecular mechanisms involved remain poorly understood. We here report the characterisation of a spontaneously arisen variant NOD mouse which displayed strongly reduced differentiation of a highly autoreactive PD-1-expressing Treg subset in the thymus. We found a nonsense mutation in the Pik3cd gene, encoding the δ-isoform of PI3K. in vitro and in vivo pharmacological inhibition of PI3Kδ and of downstream signalling through the PDK-1/AKT/mTOR pathway led to strongly reduced differentiation of PD-1+ Tregs, confirming a causative role for PI3Kδ. Mutant Tregs expressed a Treg transcriptomic signature at lower levels than WT cells. However, whereas transcriptomic and phenotypic analyses showed that PI3Kδ signalling favours expression of some genes involved in the control of Treg activity and in their suppressor effector functions, it inhibits that of others, including CTLA-4, a vital suppressor effector molecule. Thus, our data indicate that PI3Kδ signalling plays a central role in the differentiation of the functional potential of Tregs during their development in the thymus.

title: A prognostic model based on platelet-related genes accurately predicts survival in patients with gastric cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Platelets contribute to gastric cancer (GC) progression and metastasis. In this study, we aimed to construct a prognostic model based on platelet-related genes (PRGs) to predict outcomes in GC.
METHODS: RNA sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes, from which PRGs were selected as candidates. A prognostic model was built using machine learning. Immune infiltration was evaluated with CIBERSORT, and Spearman correlation was used to assess the relationships between prognostic PRGs and immune cells. Single-cell transcriptomics was used to explore cellular expression patterns, and molecular regulatory networks were constructed. The expression of candidate genes was validated in cell lines by reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR).
RESULTS: A total of 8,387 differentially expressed genes, including 123 PRGs, were identified. An eight-gene prognostic model (THPO, MMRN1, EGF, SPARC, GNAI1, CD36, SERPINE1, and ADAMTS18) was established. Distinct immune infiltration patterns were observed between risk groups, with differences in M2 macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, activated memory CD4+ T cells, regulatory T cells, and follicular helper T cells. MMRN1 expression correlated positively with monocytes (r = 0.37), whereas GNAI1 expression was negatively associated with activated memory CD4+ T cells (r =  - 0.30). Single-cell analysis showed that prognostic genes were mainly expressed in epithelial cells and fibroblasts. Two regulatory axes, SPARC-hsa-miR-494-3p-NEAT1 and GNAI1-hsa-miR-4262-NEAT1, were implicated in GC progression. RT-qPCR confirmed downregulation of CD36 and upregulation of SERPINE1 in GC tissues.
CONCLUSION: This platelet-related gene model predicts survival and immune infiltration in GC and may support the development of personalized therapies.

title: Emotional Stress as a Potential Host Factor Influencing the Efficacy of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: Mechanistic Basis and the Translation of Antidepressant Interventions.
abstract: NA: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have changed the therapeutic landscape of multiple malignancies, but primary and secondary resistance continue to limit long-term benefit. In addition to tumor-intrinsic factors, the host psychological stress state may represent a potential external variable influencing immunotherapeutic responses. Limited clinical evidence suggests that higher baseline emotional distress may be associated with poorer ICI efficacy and survival outcomes; mechanistic studies indicate that chronic stress can continuously activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system, induce elevations in glucocorticoids and catecholamines, and thereby promote CD8+ T-cell exhaustion, expansion of regulatory T cells, and PD-L1-associated immunosuppression. Some antidepressants and monoamine metabolism-related targets have shown potential in preclinical studies to remodel the tumor immune microenvironment, enhance T-cell function, and improve responses to ICIs. However, evidence concerning antidepressant-related interventions remains predominantly preclinical and hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as support for established clinical efficacy. Meanwhile, the gut microbiota and its metabolites may constitute a potential bridge between emotional state and immunotherapy. However, the existing evidence is mainly derived from observational studies and animal experiments, and heterogeneity in drug classes, confounding by indication, and differences in treatment timing all restrict direct clinical extrapolation. Overall, emotional stress may influence ICI responses through neuroendocrine-immune networks, and stratified assessment and mechanism-guided intervention centered on this potential host factor warrant further investigation.

title: Resolution of Corticosteroid-Refractory Autoimmune Hepatitis Type 1 Using a Standardized Boswellia serrata Extract: A Case Report and T-Regulatory Cell Phenotyping.
abstract: NA: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic immune-mediated liver disease typically treated with corticosteroids and azathioprine. However, some patients develop corticosteroid dependence or intolerance to conventional steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agents, highlighting the need for alternative therapeutic approaches. A 47-year-old woman with corticosteroid-dependent AIH type 1 experienced biochemical relapse during prednisolone tapering and was intolerant to both azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil. Adjunctive therapy with a standardized Boswellia serrata extract (300 mg three times daily) was initiated during a structured corticosteroid taper. Within 12 weeks, alanine aminotransferase normalized (268 to 32 U/L), immunoglobulin G decreased from 22.4 to 12.1 g/L, and prednisolone was successfully reduced from 30 to 5 mg/day without relapse. Flow cytometry demonstrated a change in the Treg/Th17 ratio from 0.4 to 1.2. Biochemical remission was maintained at 18 months without treatment-related adverse events. Standardized Boswellia serrata extract may represent a potential adjunctive steroid-sparing therapy for selected patients with refractory or treatment-intolerant autoimmune hepatitis. This observation is hypothesis-generating and does not establish causality. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm its efficacy, safety, and immunomodulatory role.

title: Regulatory T-Cell Dynamics During and After Direct Acting Antivirals in Cirrhotic HCV Genotype 4 Patients.
abstract: NA: We previously conducted longitudinal immunological studies in non-cirrhotic chronic hepatitis C patients treated with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs). However, whether cirrhosis alters these immunological dynamics remains unclear. We aimed to characterize regulatory T cells in HCV cirrhotic patients and evaluate their longitudinal changes during and following successful antiviral therapy in HCV cirrhotic patients. Fifty cirrhotic HCV genotype 4 patients and fifty age-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were analysed at baseline, week 4, end of treatment, and 1 year post-SVR using multicolour flow cytometry to quantify CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, PD-1+, and CD38+ exhausted/activated CD8+ T cells, TH1, TH2, TH17 subsets, and CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs). Longitudinal changes were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with FDR correction. At baseline, cirrhotic patients demonstrated marked immune dysregulation versus controls, with reduced CD3+ T cells, profound CD8+ T-cell exhaustion (PD-1+ 71.0% vs. 11.1%; p < 0.001), elevated CD38+ activation, depleted TH1 cells, and significant expansion of TH17 (25.8% vs. 14.0%; p < 0.001) and Tregs (52.7% vs. 15.1%; p < 0.001). Exhausted PD-1+ CD8+ cells declined by 66.2% at 1 year (q < 0.001), CD38+ CD8+ cells decreased by 31.3% (q < 0.001), and Tregs normalized (52.7%-9.6%; q < 0.001). TH1 and TH2 subsets increased, TH17 declined, and total CD3+/CD4+ T cells rose significantly by 1 year. In this single-centre cohort of compensated genotype 4 HCV-related cirrhosis, successful DAA therapy was associated with changes in circulating T-cell phenotypes, including reductions in Tregs, TH17 cells, and PD-1/CD38-expressing CD8+ T cells. These findings suggest partial improvement in peripheral immune dysregulation after viral clearance, but require confirmation in larger multicentre studies with functional assays and longer follow-up.

title: Tolerogenic Immunotherapy for Type 1 Diabetes Through Sustained Autoantigen Delivery in a Transient Inflammatory Niche.
abstract: NA: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease characterized by destruction of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in lifelong insulin therapy dependence and risk of severe complications. Tolerogenic immunotherapies offer a promising strategy to restore antigen-specific immune tolerance and prevent T1D but have been limited by challenges in controlled spatiotemporal exposure of antigens and immunomodulators to achieve robust tolerance. Here, we report the development of injectable hydrogel depot formulations providing sustained co-delivery of insulin autoantigen and low-dose interleukin-2 (IL-2) and which form transient tolerogenic niches following subcutaneous administration. These treatments recruit and expand regulatory T cells both within the hydrogel niche and draining lymph nodes, inducing tolerance responses in the spleen and pancreas and increasing the median time to diabetes onset in non-obese diabetic mice from 20 to >40 weeks. These studies suggest that sustained co-exposure of autoantigen in the appropriate immune environment can promote durable tolerance for T1D prevention.

title: Guilty by marker? Reassessing the pro-tumor reputation of antigen-presenting M2-like macrophages.
abstract: NA: M2-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are widely regarded as immunosuppressive on the basis of surface markers such as CD206 and CD163, an inference drawn largely from in vitro polarization studies rather than tested directly in the tumor-derived cells to which it is applied. This review asks what functional evidence, specifically assays of phagocytosis, antigen processing, cross-presentation, and CD8+ T cell activation, says about M2-like macrophages in cancer. A three-tier evidence framework is used to grade studies by whether they test function and whether that function is shown to be causal, applied equally to studies supporting and opposing an antitumor role for these cells. Functional evidence shows that some CD206+ or M2a-like macrophages, including ones sorted directly from tumors, can cross-present tumor antigen and activate CD8+ T cells at levels comparable with conventional type 1 dendritic cells, and that this capacity is associated with better outcomes in at least one setting. Counter-evidence shows that antigen-presenting macrophages, not always M2-like by the studies' own definitions, can instead retain cytotoxic T cells in tumor-promoting configurations or activate regulatory T cells. Across both bodies of evidence, antigen fate and co-stimulatory context are more informative about outcome than the M1/M2 marker itself. This review's claim is normative, not historical: a marker cannot by itself define function, so it cannot settle whether M2-like macrophages are pro-tumor or antitumor. Evidence is accordingly narrowed to antigen-presenting, largely CD206hi/M2a-like, macrophages, and a minimum reporting standard is proposed for future studies.

title: Ampelopsis grossedentata restores the homeostasis of Th17/Treg cells to mitigate DSS-induced ulcerative colitis through TLR1-2/NF-κB signaling pathway.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Ampelopsis grossedentata (AG), a traditional medicine from Southwest China, is frequently used to treat inflammation, anemopyretic cold, pharyngitis, hepatitis, and dysentery. Pharmacological studies confirmed that primary active constituents of AG, including flavonoids, profoundly affect anti-inflammatory processes and immunomodulation. However, the therapeutic effect and mechanisms of AG for ulcerative colitis (UC) are still unclear.
AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to elucidate the mechanisms of AG treatment of UC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: UPLC-MS and network pharmacology were employed to identify the active components of AG and their potential anti-UC mechanisms. A 4% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced UC mouse model was established for assessing therapeutic efficacy of AG based on body weight, disease activity index, colon length, and histopathology of colon tissue. RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence assays and D-lactate levels were used to evaluate the inflammatory state and epithelial barrier integrity. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometry analyses were performed to examine the underlying mechanisms. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), western blot and the TLR1/2 knockdown assays were used to identify and verify candidate targets.
RESULTS: Five flavonoids in AG were characterized via UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, with dihydromyricetin, taxifolin, myricitrin, and myricetin quantified by HPLC-DAD. Network pharmacology revealed 38 UC-related targets, enriched in IL-17/TNF signaling pathways. In vivo, AG alleviated UC-related symptoms, improved colon pathology, reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6), upregulated tight junction proteins (ZO-1, claudin 5), and inhibited the nuclear translocation of NF-κB (P65 and P50). Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometry analyses indicated that AG regulated Th17/Treg balance via the NF-κB signaling pathway. Structure-based molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, CETSA western blot and the TLR1/2 knockdown assays revealed that AG may act through the TLR1-TLR2 heterodimer receptor.
CONCLUSION: AG effectively attenuates DSS-induced UC, potentially by restoring Th17/Treg balance and inhibiting NF-κB signaling through the TLR1-TLR2 heterodimer. AG is thus a therapeutic candidate for UC treatment.

title: Regulatory T-Cell dysfunction in FOXP3-associated IPEX and selected phenocopies: mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment.
abstract: NA: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) maintain peripheral immune tolerance, with FOXP3 directing much of their differentiation and suppressive activity. Pathogenic FOXP3 variants cause immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked (IPEX) syndrome. Although often described as Treg deficiency, IPEX can occur despite preserved circulating Treg numbers and detectable FOXP3 expression. This narrative review examines how FOXP3 variants disrupt regulatory function and compares IPEX with selected genetic disorders involving BACH2, IL2RA, STAT5B, CTLA4 or LRBA. Structural and epigenetic findings are considered alongside their implications for diagnosis and treatment. The disorders are grouped by transcriptional regulation, IL-2-dependent homeostasis and checkpoint function; an IPEX-like presentation is distinguished from a defined Tregopathy. Genetic testing is central to diagnosis, while immunophenotyping and selected functional or epigenetic studies provide supporting evidence. In severe disease, investigation, stabilization and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) assessment should proceed together. HSCT remains an established potentially curative treatment. Cellular and genetic therapies are at different stages of development, from preclinical studies to early human investigation, and must be assessed individually. Comparisons with other genetic disorders and common autoimmunity help explain shared biology, but treatment findings cannot be assumed to apply equally to IPEX.

title: Role of the Tregs-Endothelial Cell Interaction Network in Immune Microenvironment Remodeling and Targeted Intervention in Cardiovascular Diseases.
abstract: NA: The pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease (CVD) involves immune and metabolic remodeling of the vascular microenvironment, in which interactions between regulatory T cells (Tregs) and endothelial cells are important. Tregs can support endothelial homeostasis through immunoregulatory cytokines, whereas endothelial signals may influence Treg activity. This network has context-dependent effects in CVD: Tregs suppress inflammation, preserve endothelial barrier integrity, and promote repair, whereas Treg dysfunction, metabolic dysregulation, or age-related changes can impair endothelial function and accelerate disease progression. This review examines how glycolysis-lactate signaling, hypoxic metabolic adaptation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and redox imbalance shape Treg-endothelial crosstalk and immune microenvironment remodeling in CVD. We also discuss molecularly targeted interventions, cell-based and engineering approaches, and metabolic therapies directed at this network. Finally, we consider how spatial and single-cell multi-omics can identify disease-associated Treg and endothelial states, map their interactions, and link transcriptional programs to metabolic dysfunction. This metabolic perspective may guide mechanistic studies and the development of targeted therapies for CVD.
